title: Understanding Capacity Planning for LLM Inference
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: In the previous part, I explored autoscaling, observability, and workload behavior using LLM-D, vLLM, Prometheus, Grafana, KEDA, and OKE Cluster Autoscaler.
The experiments made one thing very clear:

Prompt length changes prefill.

Shared context changes cache economics.

Output length changes decode occupancy.

Concurrency changes the scaling story.
The lab also showed the complete scaling chain:

Inference demand
→ more model-server pods
→ Pending pod
→ more cluster nodes
→ additional serving capacity
But that led me to another question:

How much capacity should already exist
before the traffic arrives?
Autoscaling can react to demand.

links.text: Understanding LLM-D Autoscaling, Observability, and Workload Behavior on OKE

blocks.text: Capacity planning decides how much capacity should already be available while autoscaling reacts. That was the natural handoff from Understanding LLM-D Autoscaling, Observability, and Workload Behavior on OKE.
What did I initially think capacity planning meant?
At first, I thought the calculation would be simple:

Expected traffic
÷
throughput per replica
=
number of replicas
For example:

Expected traffic = 3 requests/sec

One replica = 1 request/sec

Required replicas = 3
That sounds reasonable.
But after the experiments in Part 22, this started feeling incomplete.
One request may contain:

50 input tokens
+
50 output tokens
Another request may contain:

8000 input tokens
+
500 output tokens
Both count as:
one request
But they create completely different amounts of work.
So capacity planning for LLM inference cannot begin with request count alone.
What is capacity planning?
The mental model I am building is:

Capacity Planning
=
understand the workload
+
measure safe serving capacity
+
estimate peak demand
+
keep enough warm capacity
+
leave room for failures and scaling
The word safe is important.
The goal is not to find the maximum amount of traffic the system can accept before it crashes.
The goal is to find how much traffic it can serve while still meeting the expected user experience.
What is the difference between capacity planning and autoscaling?
Capacity planning answers:
How much capacity should already exist?
Autoscaling answers:
When should we add or remove capacity?
They work together, but they solve different problems.
A simplified flow is:

Capacity Planning
→ choose minimum warm replicas

Autoscaling
→ add replicas when demand grows

Cluster Autoscaling
→ add nodes when replicas cannot fit
In my Lab 4 setup, KEDA could request another model-server pod.
But if the cluster did not have enough CPU or memory, that pod remained Pending until OKE Cluster Autoscaler added a node.
That entire process takes time.

The Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler itself runs as a periodic control loop rather than responding continuously; the default synchronization period is 15 seconds. After that decision, Kubernetes may still need to schedule a pod, provision a node, pull an image, load the model, and wait for readiness. (Kubernetes)
So the new capacity does not appear instantly.
That is why some capacity must already be warm.
What does warm capacity mean?
Warm capacity means model-serving replicas that are:

already running
already holding model weights
already connected to the router
already ready to accept requests
For example:

Minimum replicas = 2

Current demand needs only 1 replica

Second replica remains ready
for a burst or failure
That second replica may look idle during quiet periods.
But it is also reducing the risk that users wait through the full scale-up process.
So warm capacity is not simply wasted capacity.
It is partly:

latency protection
+
failure protection
+
scale-up protection
What exactly are we planning capacity for?
This was one of the biggest clarifications for me.
We are not planning capacity for:
a model
We are planning capacity for:

a model
+
a runtime
+
a hardware configuration
+
a workload profile
+
a performance target
The same model may have very different capacity depending on:

CPU or GPU
quantization
tensor-parallel size
context length
batching configuration
prefix-cache behavior
input-token distribution
output-token distribution
request concurrency
So asking:
How many requests can this model handle?
is still not enough.
The better question is:

How many requests of this workload type
can this serving configuration handle
while meeting this latency target?
What is a workload profile?
A workload profile describes the traffic the inference service receives.
The most useful dimensions appear to be:

request arrival rate
concurrent requests
input-token length
output-token length
prefix-cache reuse
traffic burstiness

These dimensions are also reflected in modern inference benchmarking tools. For example, vLLM’s serving benchmark supports controls for request rate, maximum concurrency, input length, output length, and burstiness. (vLLM)
A useful profile may look like:

Request rate:
2 requests/sec

Prompt length:
p50 = 500 tokens
p95 = 4000 tokens

Output length:
p50 = 100 tokens
p95 = 500 tokens

Prefix-cache hit rate:
approximately 40%

Peak concurrency:
12 requests
That tells us much more than:
We expect 2 requests/sec.
Why can’t I use one throughput number?
Lab 4 made this especially visible.
With short, unique prompts, I observed approximately:

Generated throughput: 41.5 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 144 ms
With long, unique prompts:

Generated throughput: 32.4 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 764 ms
With a long reusable prefix:

KV-cache hit rate: 53%
Generated throughput: 39.9 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 172 ms
And with longer outputs:

Generated throughput: 41.7 tokens/sec
p95 TTFT: 146 ms
p95 end-to-end latency: 16 seconds
The same model server produced very different user-facing behavior depending on the workload.
This means:

Tokens/sec alone
does not describe capacity.
It needs to be interpreted together with:

TTFT
ITL
request latency
queue depth
concurrency
input length
output length
cache behavior
What should define acceptable capacity?
This leads to Service Level Objectives, or SLOs.
An example SLO might be:

p95 TTFT < 500 ms

p95 ITL < 60 ms

Error rate < 1%
These are only example values.
The correct targets depend on the application.
For an interactive chatbot, TTFT and ITL may be very important.
For an offline batch summarization workload, total throughput may matter more.
For a coding agent, long context and repeated prefixes may dominate.
So capacity should be measured against the application’s actual goal.
What is goodput?
This helped me separate two ideas.
Throughput measures:
How much work completed?
Goodput measures:

How much work completed
while still meeting the SLO?
For example:

System throughput:
2 requests/sec

Requests meeting TTFT and ITL targets:
1.5 requests/sec

Goodput:
1.5 requests/sec
NVIDIA’s GenAI-Perf documentation defines goodput as the number of completed requests per second that meet configured service-level constraints such as TTFT or inter-token latency. (NVIDIA Docs)
That means the replica’s real usable capacity is not necessarily its maximum throughput.
It is closer to:
maximum sustainable goodput
How do we find the safe capacity of one replica?
The simplest approach I understand so far is:

Fix the model, hardware, runtime configuration, and number of replicas.
Create a realistic workload profile.
Start at a low request rate or concurrency.
Increase demand gradually.
Track TTFT, ITL, queueing, errors, memory, and throughput.
Find the point where the SLO begins to degrade.
Choose an operating point below that limit.
This gives us:

Safe capacity per replica
=
highest sustained demand
that still meets the SLO
with enough operating headroom
The objective is not to reach the largest possible number.
It is to identify the region where the system remains predictable.

Performance guidance for generative-AI serving follows this same general method: benchmark representative input and output lengths, increase concurrency, and identify the point where latency begins degrading beyond the acceptable target. (NVIDIA Docs)
What is the capacity knee?
As load increases, performance may initially remain stable.
For example:

Concurrency 1:
p95 TTFT = 140 ms

Concurrency 2:
p95 TTFT = 150 ms

Concurrency 4:
p95 TTFT = 180 ms
Then the system may reach a point where latency rises much faster:

Concurrency 6:
p95 TTFT = 300 ms

Concurrency 8:
p95 TTFT = 700 ms

Concurrency 10:
p95 TTFT = 1500 ms
That sharp change is sometimes described as the knee of the curve.
Before the knee:

the system absorbs more demand
without severe degradation
After the knee:

queueing grows
latency rises quickly
the system becomes less predictable
Capacity planning should normally operate before that knee, not directly on it.
Did Lab 4 prove that one replica supports four requests?
No.
This distinction is important.
In Lab 4, the KEDA policy used:

Running-request threshold:
4 per replica
So when the system observed:
8 active requests
the calculation became:

ceil(8 / 4)
=
2 replicas
That showed that the autoscaling policy worked.
It did not prove that four active requests were the true maximum or optimal capacity of one replica.
The value was a configured scaling target.
KEDA’s AverageValue metric type works in this way: it treats the target as the desired average metric value per replica and calculates the replica count from the total metric value. (KEDA)
To validate whether 4 is a good target, I would still need to benchmark:

1 active request
2 active requests
4 active requests
6 active requests
8 active requests
...
Then observe where the selected TTFT and ITL targets begin to fail.
How are request rate and concurrency connected?
A useful approximation is:

Concurrency
≈
request arrival rate
×
average request duration
Suppose:

Arrival rate = 2 requests/sec

Average request duration = 5 seconds
Then the system may have approximately:

2 × 5
=
10 active requests
This explains why output length matters so much.
Suppose the arrival rate stays the same, but responses become longer:

Before:
2 requests/sec × 5 seconds
= 10 active requests

After:
2 requests/sec × 15 seconds
= 30 active requests
Traffic did not increase in requests per second.
But active concurrency tripled because every request stayed in the system longer.
That creates:

more decode work
more KV-cache occupancy
more active sequences
greater probability of queueing
How do we calculate the number of replicas?
Once safe capacity per replica is measured, the first estimate becomes:

Required replicas
=
ceil(
peak demand
÷
safe capacity per replica
)
For example, suppose a benchmark shows:

Safe goodput per replica:
0.8 requests/sec

Expected peak demand:
2 requests/sec
Then:

ceil(2 / 0.8)
=
ceil(2.5)
=
3 replicas
We can also calculate using validated active concurrency:

Required replicas
=
ceil(
expected peak active requests
÷
safe active requests per replica
)
Suppose:

Peak active requests = 10

Validated safe active requests
per replica = 4
Then:

ceil(10 / 4)
=
3 replicas
These are starting estimates.
They do not yet include failures, bursts, or scale-up delay.
Why do we need headroom?
Running at 100% of measured capacity leaves no room for variation.
Real traffic contains:

long-tail prompts
longer-than-expected outputs
cache misses
temporary traffic bursts
replica failures
node failures
model reloads
routing imbalance
forecasting errors
So I now think about several types of headroom:

Performance headroom
=
avoid operating at the capacity knee

Burst headroom
=
absorb short traffic spikes

Failure headroom
=
continue serving when a replica fails

Scale-up headroom
=
serve traffic while new capacity starts
The exact amount is a business and engineering decision.
There is no universal percentage that works for every inference service.
What is N+1 capacity?
One simple availability policy is:

Required for demand = N replicas

Keep one additional replica = N + 1
For example:

Normal peak requires 3 replicas.

Warm capacity = 4 replicas.
If one replica fails:
3 replicas remain
and the expected peak workload can still be served.
But N+1 is only one policy.
For larger deployments, operators may plan for:

one node failure
one availability-domain failure
multiple replica failures
regional failover
The capacity model should reflect the actual failure scenario the system needs to tolerate.
How do replicas translate into nodes?
Once the replica count is known, I still need to determine where those replicas will run.
A simplified calculation is:

Pods per node
=
minimum of:

allocatable CPU ÷ pod CPU request

allocatable memory ÷ pod memory request

available accelerators ÷ accelerators per pod
Then:

Required nodes
=
ceil(
required replicas
÷
pods per node
)
Suppose one node can safely fit:
2 model-server replicas
And warm capacity requires:
5 replicas
Then:

ceil(5 / 2)
=
3 nodes
This calculation should use allocatable resources, not the node’s full advertised resources.
Kubernetes, networking components, monitoring agents, and other system workloads also need capacity.
For GPU deployments, topology may become another constraint.
A replica may require:

1 GPU
4 GPUs using tensor parallelism
or
multiple nodes
So the scheduling unit may be much larger than one pod on one GPU.
How does scale-up time affect capacity?
Suppose the service currently has warm capacity for:
1 request/sec
Traffic suddenly rises to:
2 requests/sec
And additional capacity takes:
60 seconds
to become ready.
A simplified estimate of temporary backlog growth is:

Backlog
≈
(incoming rate - warm service rate)
×
scale-up time
So:

(2 - 1) requests/sec
×
60 seconds
=
approximately 60 queued requests
This is a simplified model.
Real systems also have variable request duration, batching, and partial completions.
But it makes the basic risk visible.
Even if autoscaling eventually adds enough capacity, users arriving during that minute may already experience poor TTFT or timeouts.
How much warm capacity should we keep?
The answer depends partly on how much queueing the application can tolerate.
An interactive assistant may need:

more warm capacity
faster scale-up
stricter TTFT protection
A batch-processing service may tolerate:

more queueing
slower scale-up
higher utilization
The basic tradeoff is:

More warm capacity
=
higher cost
+
lower latency risk

Less warm capacity
=
lower idle cost
+
greater scale-up and queueing risk
Capacity planning is therefore not purely a performance calculation.
It is also a cost and reliability decision.
How do capacity planning and autoscaling fit together?
The mental model I now have is:

Warm capacity
handles immediate expected demand.

Pod autoscaling
handles sustained demand growth.

Node autoscaling
creates infrastructure for new pods.

Admission control
protects the service
when demand exceeds all available capacity.
These layers should not be treated as independent features.
They are parts of one capacity system.
Can one model have multiple capacity profiles?
Yes.
This may be one of the most important lessons.
The same model can have different capacity profiles for:

Interactive chat

Long-context RAG

Coding assistants

Agentic workflows

Offline batch processing
For example:

Interactive chat:
short prompts
medium outputs
strict TTFT

RAG:
long prompts
short outputs
possible prefix reuse

Creative writing:
short prompts
very long outputs
decode-heavy

Document summarization:
long prompts
long outputs
high total occupancy
Trying to combine all of these into one average request can hide the real bottlenecks.
It may be better to create:

separate workload classes
separate benchmark profiles
possibly separate serving pools
What would a practical capacity-planning process look like?
The process I would follow now is:

1. Define workload classes.

2. Measure prompt-length distributions.

3. Measure output-length distributions.

4. Measure arrival rate,
   concurrency, and burstiness.

5. Define TTFT, ITL,
   error-rate, and throughput targets.

6. Benchmark one replica
   with realistic workloads.

7. Find the SLO-safe capacity point.

8. Forecast normal and peak demand.

9. Calculate required replicas.

10. Add burst, failure,
    and scale-up headroom.

11. Map replicas to nodes.

12. Measure real pod and node
    scale-up times.

13. Run a full-system load test.

14. Compare prediction
    with production measurements.
The last step matters.
Capacity planning is not something we calculate once and finish.
The estimates should be compared with real behavior and adjusted continuously.
How does this change how I interpret Lab 4?
During the concurrent workload, I observed approximately:

Running requests: 8
Waiting requests: 0

p95 TTFT: 236 ms
p95 ITL: 50 ms

Request throughput:
0.74 requests/sec
KEDA requested another replica because the configured threshold was:
4 running requests per replica
This was a successful autoscaling experiment.
But it was only one point on the performance curve.
To turn that experiment into a real capacity plan, the next step would be:

Choose an SLO.

Hold the deployment at one replica.

Increase request rate gradually.

Repeat across:
- short unique prompts
- long unique prompts
- shared-prefix prompts
- long outputs
- realistic mixed traffic

Find where p95 TTFT,
p95 ITL, queue depth,
or errors cross the target.

Set the scaling threshold
before that point.
That would turn:
4 active requests per replica
from a configured assumption into a measured operating target.
What is the biggest mental shift?
Before exploring this, I thought capacity planning was mainly:

Peak requests
÷
maximum throughput
=
replicas
Now the picture looks more like:

Workload shape
determines per-request work.

SLO
defines acceptable performance.

Benchmarking
finds safe replica capacity.

Demand forecasting
estimates required replicas.

Scale-up time and failures
determine headroom.

Cost
influences how much capacity stays warm.
So the final number is not simply a hardware calculation.
It is the result of several connected decisions.
What is the key intuition?
The simplest summary is:

Benchmarking tells me
what one replica can safely do.

Capacity planning tells me
how many replicas should already exist.

Autoscaling tells the system
when to add or remove replicas.

Cluster autoscaling tells Kubernetes
where those replicas can run.
And the deeper lesson is:

Capacity is not the maximum load
the system can survive.

Capacity is the load
the system can serve reliably
while meeting the user experience target.
What comes next?
Now that the capacity-planning mental model is clearer, the next question becomes:

Which live metrics should trigger scaling
before users experience a problem?
Should we scale on:

active requests
queue depth
TTFT
ITL
KV-cache pressure
token backlog
goodput
And which of these are early signals versus signals that tell us the system is already unhealthy?
That leads naturally to:
LLM Inference Challenges
Understanding SLO-Driven Autoscaling for LLM Inference
Because capacity planning decides the starting point.
The next challenge is making the system react early enough to protect that capacity plan when real traffic behaves differently from the forecast.
